title: The Proposition
full_review:
Lovers of Westerns and Australian films may have the stomach for the artful but unsparing 1880s-era Outback saga, "The Proposition" (First Look), but be warned: This is strong stuff.

Capt. Stanley (Ray Winstone), a British law enforcement officer, is hoping to bring order to the lawless area, while protecting his delicate wife, Martha (Emily Watson), from the harsh realities of his job.

Having captured two of the three notorious Burns gang members, Stanley offers one of them, Charlie (Guy Pearce), the chance to save the life of his jailed kid brother, Mikey (Richard Wilson). This is provided that Charlie finds and kills their ringleader, savage older brother Arthur (Danny Huston), wanted for the murder of a pregnant woman.

Stanley's unorthodox proposition greets the ear of landowner Eden Fletcher (David Wenham), who, against Stanley's wishes, has the whimpering Mikey taken out and viciously whipped in front of the townspeople, including -- surprisingly -- Martha, who wants to see justice done for the sake of the murdered woman who had been her friend. (She regrets the decision when watching the sickening scourging.)

Meanwhile, Charlie does find his poetry-spouting renegade brother, who saves Charlie from an attack by Aborigines. The act derails Charlie's resolve.

But there will be plenty of brutality and bloodshed to come, including an ugly episode with a vicious bounty hunter, Jellon Lamb (John Hurt).

Director John Hillcoat, working from a minimalist script by musician Nick Cave, creates the requisite desolate ambience, and the performances are first-rate.

The film, sometimes absorbing but more often tedious, pays homage to classic Western themes, and its portrayal of the Aborigines can be viewed as somewhat analogous to that of the American Indian. The film is not without moral complexity as nearly all the characters are faced with ethical dilemmas and the line between "good" and "bad" is very fine.

But for all its metaphorical purpose ("nation-building founded on violence" is how Hillcoat has described it), the intense savagery in this gritty, somber tale will not be to every taste.

This film contains pervasive brutality and violence, beatings, murder, rough language and a nongraphic but disturbing rape. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
